paper.title: Chemistry Higher Paper 1: Mock 1
paper.instructions: You may use a calculator. Answer all the questions. Relative atomic masses are given in the questions where you need them. Show your working in calculations: you can get marks for method even if your final answer is wrong. Questions marked 6 marks are extended answers: write in full sentences and organise your ideas. Diagrams are described in words; you can describe any diagram you would draw.

questions.topic: Atomic Structure and the Periodic Table
questions.subtopic: Subatomic particles, isotopes and relative atomic mass
questions.question_text:
This question is about magnesium. The atomic number of magnesium is 12.

(a) An atom of magnesium has a mass number of 25. Give the number of protons, neutrons and electrons in this atom. (2 marks)

(b) What are isotopes? (1 mark)

(c) A sample of magnesium contains:
79% magnesium-24
10% magnesium-25
11% magnesium-26

Calculate the relative atomic mass (Ar) of magnesium in this sample. Give your answer to 1 decimal place. Show your working. (3 marks)

(d) Give the electronic structure of a magnesium atom and of a magnesium ion, Mg²⁺. (2 marks)

points: (a) 12 protons and 12 electrons
(a) 13 neutrons
(b) Atoms of the same element with the same number of protons but different numbers of neutrons
(c) Multiplies each mass number by its abundance: (24 × 79) + (25 × 10) + (26 × 11) = 2432
(d) Magnesium atom: 2,8,2
(d) Magnesium ion: 2,8
scheme.guidance: In (b), 'different mass number' is acceptable for different numbers of neutrons. In (c), 24.32 not rounded scores 2 of the 3 marks. This question asks for working. A correct final answer with no working scores only the mark(s) for the answer itself, not the method marks. Award each method mark when that step is shown. If the working has a slip (e.g. a wrong number copied) but the final answer is correct, withhold only the mark(s) for the step that is wrong.

questions.topic: Atomic Structure and the Periodic Table
questions.question_text:
This question is about the elements in Group 7 and Group 0.

(a) A student adds chlorine water to colourless potassium bromide solution.

(i) Describe what the student would see. (1 mark)
(ii) Write a balanced symbol equation for the reaction. (2 marks)

(b) Explain why chlorine is more reactive than bromine. Answer in terms of electrons. (3 marks)

(c) Explain why the noble gases in Group 0 are unreactive. (2 marks)

points: (a)(i) The solution turns orange (or yellow/brown)
(a)(ii) Correct formulae: Cl₂ + KBr → KCl + Br₂
(a)(ii) Correctly balanced: Cl₂ + 2KBr → 2KCl + Br₂
(b) A chlorine atom is smaller / has fewer electron shells than a bromine atom
(b) So the outer shell is closer to the nucleus and there is a stronger attraction to the nucleus (less shielding)
(b) So chlorine gains an electron more easily
(c) Noble gases have a full (stable) outer shell of electrons (8, or 2 for helium)
(c) So they do not easily lose, gain or share electrons
scheme.guidance: In (b), do not credit 'loses electrons more easily' or answers about the reactivity of Group 1. 'Bromine is displaced' alone does not answer (b).

questions.topic: Atomic Structure and the Periodic Table
questions.subtopic: The periodic table, metals and non-metals
questions.question_text:
Before the discovery of protons, neutrons and electrons, scientists tried to classify the elements by arranging them in order of their atomic weights.

Explain how Mendeleev developed his periodic table, and why it came to be accepted by other scientists.

(6 marks)

levels.descriptor: A clear, detailed and logically ordered explanation covering how Mendeleev arranged the elements, why he left gaps or changed the order, and why the table was accepted, including the later discovery of predicted elements and/or isotopes.
Some explanation of how the table was arranged and at least one reason it was accepted, with some detail.
Simple statements about early periodic tables or Mendeleev, with little explanation.

indicative: Early tables ordered elements only by atomic weight, so some elements were put in groups with the wrong properties, and new elements had no place
Mendeleev arranged elements mainly by atomic weight, but grouped elements with similar properties together
He changed the order of some pairs of elements (e.g. tellurium and iodine) so they fitted the properties of their groups
He left gaps for elements that he thought had not yet been discovered
He used the gaps to predict the properties of undiscovered elements
When elements such as gallium and germanium were discovered, their properties matched his predictions, so scientists accepted the table
Later, the discovery of isotopes and of protons explained why ordering by atomic weight was not always correct: the modern table is ordered by atomic number
scheme.guidance: Level 3 needs both how the table was developed and why it was accepted.

questions.question_text:
This question is about bonding.

(a) Sodium reacts with oxygen to form sodium oxide, an ionic compound.

Describe what happens to the electrons when sodium oxide forms, and give the formula of sodium oxide. Sodium is in Group 1 and oxygen is in Group 6. You may describe a dot and cross diagram in words. (5 marks)

(b) Methane, CH₄, is a covalent substance.

(i) What is a covalent bond? (1 mark)
(ii) Explain why methane has a low boiling point. (2 marks)

points: (a) Each sodium atom loses one electron (from its outer shell)
(a) Each oxygen atom gains two electrons
(a) Two sodium atoms are needed for each oxygen atom
(a) Forming Na⁺ and O²⁻ ions, which have full outer shells (the electronic structure of a noble gas)
(a) Formula Na₂O
(b)(i) A shared pair of electrons between two atoms
(b)(ii) Methane is made of small molecules with weak forces between the molecules (intermolecular forces)
(b)(ii) Little energy is needed to overcome these forces (the covalent bonds do not break when it boils)
scheme.guidance: In (a), 'oxygen shares electrons with sodium' scores 0 for the electron transfer marks. In (b)(ii), 'the covalent bonds are weak' or 'the bonds break' scores 0.

questions.subtopic: Small molecules, polymers and giant covalent structures
questions.question_text:
This question is about substances with different structures.

(a) Silicon dioxide (silica) melts at about 1700 °C. Explain why silicon dioxide has a very high melting point. (3 marks)

(b) Poly(ethene) is a polymer. Explain why poly(ethene) is a solid at room temperature but ethene is a gas. (2 marks)

(c) Buckminsterfullerene is a molecule made of carbon atoms. Give its molecular formula, and give one use of carbon nanotubes. (2 marks)

points: (a) Silicon dioxide has a giant covalent structure (lattice)
(a) There are many strong covalent bonds between the atoms
(a) A lot of energy is needed to break these bonds
(b) Poly(ethene) molecules are very large / long chains
(b) So the intermolecular forces between them are stronger than between small ethene molecules (more energy needed to overcome them)
(c) C₆₀
(c) A valid use of nanotubes, e.g. in electronics, to reinforce materials such as tennis rackets, or in nanotechnology
scheme.guidance: In (a), any mention of intermolecular forces scores 0 for the second and third marks.

questions.question_text:
This question is about metals, alloys and nanoparticles.

(a) Pure copper is soft and can be bent into shape. Explain why. (2 marks)

(b) Brass is an alloy of copper and zinc. Explain why brass is harder than pure copper. (3 marks)

(c) Some socks contain silver nanoparticles, which kill bacteria.

(i) Give the size range of nanoparticles. (1 mark)
(ii) Explain why only a small mass of silver is needed when it is used as nanoparticles. (1 mark)
(iii) Give one possible risk of using nanoparticles in products like socks. (1 mark)

points: (a) Copper atoms are arranged in layers
(a) The layers can slide over each other
(b) Brass contains atoms of different sizes (zinc and copper)
(b) The different sized atoms distort the layers
(b) So the layers cannot slide over each other as easily
(c)(i) 1 to 100 nanometres (1 × 10⁻⁹ m to 1 × 10⁻⁷ m)
(c)(ii) Nanoparticles have a very high surface area to volume ratio
(c)(iii) A valid risk, e.g. their effects on health are not fully known, they could be breathed in or absorbed, or they could be washed into the environment
scheme.guidance: In (a), 'the atoms slide' without layers can score the second mark only. In (b), 'zinc makes it stronger' alone scores 0.

questions.subtopic: Moles, reacting masses and limiting reactants
questions.question_text:
Magnesium burns in oxygen to form magnesium oxide:

2Mg + O₂ → 2MgO

Relative atomic masses (Ar): Mg = 24, O = 16

(a) Calculate the relative formula mass (Mr) of magnesium oxide. (1 mark)

(b) A student heats 0.36 g of magnesium in a crucible. The mass of the contents of the crucible increases. Explain why, even though mass is conserved in chemical reactions. (2 marks)

(c) Calculate the maximum mass of magnesium oxide that could be made from 0.36 g of magnesium. Show your working. (3 marks)

(d) The student made 0.51 g of magnesium oxide. Calculate the percentage yield. Show your working. (2 marks)

(e) In another experiment, 4.8 g of magnesium is burned with 2.4 g of oxygen. Determine which reactant is the limiting reactant. Show your working. (3 marks)

points: (a) Mr of MgO = 40
(b) Oxygen from the air combines with the magnesium
(b) The mass of the oxygen that has reacted is added to the mass of the magnesium (the oxygen was not weighed at the start)
(c) Moles of Mg = 0.36 ÷ 24 = 0.015 mol
(c) Moles of MgO = 0.015 mol (2 : 2 ratio)
(c) Mass of MgO = 0.015 × 40 = 0.60 g
(d) Percentage yield = 0.51 ÷ 0.60 × 100
(e) Moles of Mg = 4.8 ÷ 24 = 0.2 mol and moles of O₂ = 2.4 ÷ 32 = 0.075 mol
(e) 0.2 mol of Mg needs 0.1 mol of O₂ (2 : 1 ratio)
(e) There is only 0.075 mol of O₂, so oxygen is the limiting reactant
scheme.guidance: Allow error carried forward in (c) to (d). In (e), using Mr = 16 for oxygen gives 0.15 mol and can score the ratio mark, but the conclusion must follow from the student's numbers. 'Oxygen' with no working scores the final mark only. This question asks for working. A correct final answer with no working scores only the mark(s) for the answer itself, not the method marks. Award each method mark when that step is shown. If the working has a slip (e.g. a wrong number copied) but the final answer is correct, withhold only the mark(s) for the step that is wrong.

questions.question_text:
Hydrogen can be made by reacting methane with steam:

CH₄ + H₂O → CO + 3H₂

Relative formula masses (Mr): CH₄ = 16, H₂O = 18, CO = 28, H₂ = 2

(a) Calculate the percentage atom economy for making hydrogen by this reaction. Give your answer to 3 significant figures. Show your working. (3 marks)

(b) Give two reasons why chemical companies try to use reactions with a high atom economy. (2 marks)

(c) 1 mole of any gas occupies 24 dm³ at room temperature and pressure. Calculate the volume of hydrogen, at room temperature and pressure, made from 8.0 g of methane. Show your working. (3 marks)

points: (a) Total Mr of reactants = 16 + 18 = 34
(a) Mr of desired product = 3 × 2 = 6, and atom economy = 6 ÷ 34 × 100
(b) Less waste is produced
(b) A second valid reason, e.g. it uses fewer resources, is more sustainable, or is cheaper / more profitable
(c) Moles of CH₄ = 8.0 ÷ 16 = 0.5 mol
(c) Moles of H₂ = 0.5 × 3 = 1.5 mol
(c) Volume = 1.5 × 24 = 36 dm³
scheme.guidance: In (a), using 2 instead of 6 for hydrogen (5.88%) can score the first mark only. In (c), allow error carried forward from a wrong number of moles. This question asks for working. A correct final answer with no working scores only the mark(s) for the answer itself, not the method marks. Award each method mark when that step is shown. If the working has a slip (e.g. a wrong number copied) but the final answer is correct, withhold only the mark(s) for the step that is wrong.

questions.subtopic: Reactions of acids, salts and neutralisation
questions.question_text:
This question is about acids.

(a) Name the salt made when zinc oxide reacts with hydrochloric acid. (1 mark)

(b) Zinc metal reacts with hydrochloric acid to make a salt and hydrogen. Write a balanced symbol equation for this reaction. (2 marks)

(c) In this reaction, zinc atoms are oxidised. Write a half equation for the zinc, and explain why this is oxidation. (2 marks)

(d) A student has solutions of hydrochloric acid and ethanoic acid with the same concentration. The hydrochloric acid has a lower pH. Explain why. (3 marks)

(e) The pH of an acid solution changes from 3 to 1. By what factor does the concentration of hydrogen ions increase? (1 mark)

points: (a) Zinc chloride
(b) Correct formulae: Zn + HCl → ZnCl₂ + H₂
(b) Correctly balanced: Zn + 2HCl → ZnCl₂ + H₂
(c) Zn → Zn²⁺ + 2e⁻
(c) It is oxidation because zinc loses electrons
(d) Hydrochloric acid is a strong acid: it is completely ionised in water
(d) Ethanoic acid is a weak acid: it is only partially ionised
(d) So hydrochloric acid has a higher concentration of hydrogen ions (H⁺), giving a lower pH
(e) 100 (times)
scheme.guidance: In (d), answers saying hydrochloric acid is 'more concentrated' score 0 for that idea: the concentrations are the same. In (c), accept Zn − 2e⁻ → Zn²⁺.

questions.subtopic: Reactions of acids, salts and neutralisation
questions.question_text:
Copper sulfate is a soluble salt. It can be made by reacting copper oxide, an insoluble solid, with dilute sulfuric acid.

Describe a method to make pure, dry crystals of copper sulfate from copper oxide and dilute sulfuric acid.

(6 marks)

levels.descriptor: A coherent, logically ordered method that would produce pure, dry crystals, including adding excess copper oxide, filtering, and crystallising, with relevant detail and safety.
The main steps of a method are given, but with some steps missing or out of order, or with little detail; the method would produce crystals but they might not be pure or dry.
Simple, disconnected statements about making a salt, with little chance of producing crystals.

indicative: Measure a volume of dilute sulfuric acid into a beaker
Warm the acid gently (to speed up the reaction)
Add copper oxide a little at a time, stirring, until no more dissolves (excess copper oxide), so all the acid has reacted
Filter the mixture to remove the excess copper oxide
Heat the filtrate (copper sulfate solution) in an evaporating basin to evaporate some of the water, until crystals start to form
Leave the solution to cool and crystallise
Remove the crystals, e.g. by filtering, and dry them between filter paper or in a warm oven
Wear eye protection; avoid boiling the solution dry
scheme.guidance: To reach Level 3 the method must use excess copper oxide and filtering before crystallising. Heating to dryness can still reach Level 2.

questions.question_text:
A solution of sodium chloride in water is electrolysed using inert electrodes.

(a) Name the product formed at the negative electrode and the product formed at the positive electrode. (2 marks)

(b) Explain why sodium is not produced at the negative electrode. (2 marks)

(c) Write a balanced half equation for the reaction at the positive electrode. (2 marks)

(d) Explain why the solution left at the end contains sodium hydroxide. (2 marks)

points: (a) Negative electrode: hydrogen
(a) Positive electrode: chlorine
(b) Sodium is more reactive than hydrogen
(b) So hydrogen ions (from the water) are discharged instead of sodium ions
(c) Correct species: Cl⁻ → Cl₂ + e⁻
(c) Correctly balanced: 2Cl⁻ → Cl₂ + 2e⁻
(d) Hydrogen ions and chloride ions are removed from the solution as hydrogen and chlorine
(d) Sodium ions and hydroxide ions are left in the solution

questions.subtopic: Exothermic and endothermic reactions and reaction profiles
questions.question_text:
A student mixes dilute hydrochloric acid with sodium hydroxide solution in a polystyrene cup. The temperature rises from 21 °C to 29 °C.

(a) Is the reaction exothermic or endothermic? Give a reason for your answer. (2 marks)

(b) Describe the reaction profile for this reaction. Include the activation energy and the overall energy change in your description. (3 marks)

(c) Explain, in terms of breaking and making bonds, why this reaction is exothermic. (2 marks)

points: (a) Exothermic
(a) Because the temperature increased (energy is transferred to the surroundings)
(b) The products are at a lower energy level than the reactants
(b) The activation energy is the rise from the reactants up to the peak of the curve
(b) The overall energy change is the drop from the reactants to the products (energy released)
(c) Energy is needed to break bonds and energy is released when bonds form
(c) More energy is released making the new bonds than is needed to break the old bonds
scheme.guidance: In (a), the reason mark depends on choosing exothermic. In (c), 'breaking bonds releases energy' scores 0 for the first mark.

questions.question_text:
Some electric cars are powered by hydrogen fuel cells. Others are powered by rechargeable lithium-ion batteries.

Evaluate the use of hydrogen fuel cells compared with rechargeable batteries to power cars.

(6 marks)

levels.descriptor: A balanced evaluation with several advantages and disadvantages of both, clearly compared, and a reasoned conclusion.
Some advantages and/or disadvantages of both, or a detailed account of one; a conclusion may be missing or unsupported.
Simple statements about fuel cells or batteries, with little comparison.

indicative: Fuel cells: the only product is water, so no pollution at the point of use
Fuel cells keep producing electricity as long as hydrogen is supplied, and refuelling is quick
Fuel cells do not need to be recharged and do not wear out as quickly as batteries
Hydrogen is a flammable gas that is difficult to store safely and needs high pressure
Hydrogen is often made from fossil fuels (e.g. methane) or by electrolysis, which needs energy
There are few hydrogen filling stations
Batteries: recharging takes a long time but can be done at home; there are many charging points
Batteries eventually lose their capacity, and they contain toxic or scarce metals that are hard to dispose of or recycle
Electricity to recharge batteries may come from fossil fuel power stations
Conclusion weighing up the points
scheme.guidance: Level 3 needs both technologies and a conclusion.
